```{r}
#| label: setup

library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)

# Must match the --id you passed to qualtrics/export-data.js (data/raw/<id>/responses.csv).
# Phase 2 runs under its own id, so its data never mix with Phase 1's.
experiment_id        <- "yin2024-label-pilot-b"
```

```{r}
#| label: original-study
#| include: false
# The original study's numbers, entered once and used by the power analysis, the Key
# statistics table, and the side-by-side figures.
#
# This replication shows only AI-generated responses, so the matching original comparison is the
# label effect WITHIN the AI-response conditions (Yin, Jia & Wakslak, 2024, Table 2, p. 5):
#   AI response, AI label      M = 5.41, SD = 1.33
#   AI response, human label   M = 6.12, SD = 0.97
# (NOT Table 1's label means, 5.13 vs 5.81, which pool AI and human responses.)
# Cell sizes are not in the paper. They come from the authors' public data on OSF
# (https://osf.io/8wnmr, "Being Heard by AI OSF.csv"), which reproduces Tables 1 and 2 exactly:
# AI response / AI label n = 124, AI response / human label n = 110.
# The paper's own test of this contrast (SI Table 2): t(451) = 4.00, p < .001, d = 0.52, 95% CI
# [0.31, 0.74], using the error variance pooled over all four cells.
original <- tibble(
  condition = c("ai", "human"),
  n         = c(124, 110),
  mean      = c(5.41, 6.12),
  sd        = c(1.33, 0.97)
)

# All four outcomes in the same cells (AI responses; AI label n = 124, human label n = 110).
# Means and SDs are the paper's Table 2 (p. 5); the cell sizes are from the OSF data. (The raw OSF
# data give 6.05 / 1.19 for accuracy in the human-label cell, a last-digit rounding difference.)
# The measure names match the columns of the exported ratings rows.
original_measures <- tribble(
  ~measure,                ~condition, ~n,  ~mean, ~sd,
  "feeling_heard",         "ai",       124, 5.41,  1.33,
  "feeling_heard",         "human",    110, 6.12,  0.97,
  "response_accuracy",     "ai",       124, 5.81,  1.18,
  "response_accuracy",     "human",    110, 6.06,  1.02,
  "responder_understood",  "ai",       124, 5.43,  1.47,
  "responder_understood",  "human",    110, 6.19,  0.92,
  "connection",            "ai",       124, 4.28,  1.80,
  "connection",            "human",    110, 5.19,  1.18
)
```

One row per study for the key comparison: the original, your Phase 1 replication, and your
Phase 2 extension. The table fills itself in from the data as each phase is exported, using the

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"
# Load one phase's exported data and apply the exclusion rules of the analysis plan. Returns NULL if
# that phase has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows to skip itself.
# The data come from Qualtrics (qualtrics/export-data.js): one row per response, numeric answers only.
# Qualtrics preview and test responses are already dropped by the export script.
read_phase <- function(id) {
  path <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id, "responses.csv")
  if (!file.exists(path)) return(NULL)
  d <- read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)

  heard_items <- c("heard_understood", "heard_validated", "heard_affirmed", "heard_seen",
                   "heard_accepted", "heard_cared_for")
  acc_items   <- c("acc_captures", "acc_summarizes")
  und_items   <- c("und_knew", "und_understood")
  conn_items  <- c("conn_close", "conn_connected", "conn_trust")
  # A participant who stopped before a screen has no answers, so make sure every column exists.
  for (col in c("Finished", "consent", "label", "desc_words", "reply_n_words", "tech_issues",
                heard_items, acc_items, und_items, conn_items)) {
    if (!col %in% names(d)) d[[col]] <- NA
  }
  # A composite is the mean of its items, and missing unless every item was answered.
  scale_mean <- function(df, cols) {
    m <- as.matrix(df[, cols])
    ifelse(rowSums(is.na(m)) == 0, rowMeans(m), NA_real_)
  }
  d <- d |>
    mutate(completed = coalesce(as.numeric(Finished) == 1, FALSE),
           consented = coalesce(as.numeric(consent) == 1, FALSE),
           condition = label,
           feeling_heard        = scale_mean(d, heard_items),
           response_accuracy    = scale_mean(d, acc_items),
           responder_understood = scale_mean(d, und_items),
           connection           = scale_mean(d, conn_items))

  # Exclusion rules (the analysis plan): a participant is analysed only if they finished the survey,
  # gave valid consent, wrote a description of at least 30 words (the interface already refuses shorter
  # ones), and answered all six feeling-heard items (so the mean can be computed). Each participant
  # is counted under the FIRST rule they fail, in the order below.
  min_words <- 30
  status <- d |>
    mutate(reason = case_when(
      !completed                                         ~ "Did not finish the survey",
      !consented                                         ~ "No valid consent",
      coalesce(as.numeric(desc_words), 0) < min_words    ~ "Description under 30 words",
      is.na(feeling_heard)                               ~ "Missing one of the six feeling-heard items",
      TRUE                                               ~ "Analysed"))
  keep <- status |> filter(reason == "Analysed")
  scores <- keep |> select(participant_id, condition, feeling_heard, response_accuracy,
                           responder_understood, connection)

  list(participants = d, complete = filter(d, completed), keep = keep, scores = scores, status = status,
       n_test = 0L,  # preview / test responses are removed by qualtrics/export-data.js before this file is written
       n_no_score = sum(status$reason == "Missing one of the six feeling-heard items"))
}

# One row per label condition for the analysed participants: n, mean and SD of a measure.
label_summary <- function(d, var = "feeling_heard") {
  d$scores |>
    group_by(condition) |>
    summarise(n = sum(!is.na(.data[[var]])), mean = mean(.data[[var]], na.rm = TRUE),
              sd = sd(.data[[var]], na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
}

# The key statistic: difference in mean Feeling Heard (AI label minus human label) with a 95%
# CI from Welch's t test, plus Cohen's d (pooled SD). Works from the per-condition summary,
# so the original (summary statistics only) and the replication go through the same code.
# NULL until both labels have at least two analysed participants (and some variation).
diff_ci <- function(s) {
  ai <- s[s$condition == "ai", ]
  hu <- s[s$condition == "human", ]
  if (nrow(ai) == 0 || nrow(hu) == 0 || ai$n < 2 || hu$n < 2 || anyNA(c(ai$sd, hu$sd))) return(NULL)
  # No variation in either group (for example everyone gave the same rating): the test is undefined.
  if (ai$sd == 0 && hu$sd == 0) return(NULL)
  v_ai <- ai$sd^2 / ai$n
  v_hu <- hu$sd^2 / hu$n
  se   <- sqrt(v_ai + v_hu)
  df   <- (v_ai + v_hu)^2 / (v_ai^2 / (ai$n - 1) + v_hu^2 / (hu$n - 1))
  est  <- ai$mean - hu$mean
  sd_p <- sqrt(((ai$n - 1) * ai$sd^2 + (hu$n - 1) * hu$sd^2) / (ai$n + hu$n - 2))
  tibble(N = ai$n + hu$n, estimate = est,
         ci_low = est - qt(.975, df) * se, ci_high = est + qt(.975, df) * se,
         statistic = est / se, df = df, p = 2 * pt(-abs(est / se), df), d = est / sd_p,
         # Approximate 95% CI for d (large-sample standard error).
         d_low  = est / sd_p - 1.96 * sqrt((ai$n + hu$n) / (ai$n * hu$n) + (est / sd_p)^2 / (2 * (ai$n + hu$n))),
         d_high = est / sd_p + 1.96 * sqrt((ai$n + hu$n) / (ai$n * hu$n) + (est / sd_p)^2 / (2 * (ai$n + hu$n))))
}

# Side-by-side figure: any number of studies on the same axes, in the order given. Each
# argument is a per-condition summary (condition, n, mean, sd).
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    mutate(half = qt(.975, n - 1) * sd / sqrt(n),
           Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)),
           label = sprintf("n = %d", n),
           condition = factor(condition, levels = c("ai", "human"), labels = c("AI label", "Human label")))
  fills <- setNames(c("grey55", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.8)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = condition, y = mean, fill = Study)) +
    geom_col(position = dodge, width = 0.75) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - half, ymax = mean + half), position = dodge, width = 0.2) +
    geom_text(aes(y = 1.1, label = label), position = dodge, vjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "white") +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1, 7)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:7) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = fills) +
    labs(x = "Label", y = "Feeling Heard (1-7)", fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
}

# The four outcomes of the original, in its order.
measure_labels <- c(feeling_heard = "Feeling heard", response_accuracy = "Response accuracy",
                    responder_understood = "Responder understood me", connection = "Connection to responder")

# n, mean and SD by label for each of the four outcomes (the replication's analysed participants).
measure_summaries <- function(d) {
  map_dfr(names(measure_labels), ~ label_summary(d, .x) |> mutate(measure = .x))
}
# The label effect (AI minus human label) with its 95% CI for each outcome. Same code for the
# original (original_measures) and the replication; outcomes with fewer than two per label are dropped.
measure_effects <- function(summ) {
  map_dfr(unique(summ$measure), function(m) {
    r <- diff_ci(summ[summ$measure == m, ])
    if (is.null(r)) NULL else mutate(r, measure = m)
  })
}
# Label effects for the four outcomes, studies side by side, with 95% CIs.
effects_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    mutate(measure = factor(measure_labels[measure], levels = measure_labels),
           Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)))
  ggplot(df, aes(x = measure, y = estimate, colour = Study)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
    geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey40", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)]) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Difference in mean rating (AI label \u2212 human label)", colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 12, hjust = 1))
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
fmt_row <- function(study, r) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `Effect (AI − human label)` = "not yet collected",
                  `95% CI` = "", `t(df)` = "", d = "", p = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Effect (AI − human label)` = sprintf("%.2f points", r$estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", r$ci_low, r$ci_high),
         `t(df)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.0f)", r$statistic, r$df),
         d = sprintf("%.2f", r$d),
         p = format.pval(r$p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001))
}
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original", diff_ci(original)),
  fmt_row("Phase 1: replication", if (have_data) diff_ci(label_summary(phase1))),
  fmt_row("Phase 2: extension", if (have_phase2) diff_ci(label_summary(phase2)))
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrllllr",
               caption = "Key comparison: Feeling Heard (1-7), AI label minus human label, Welch t test.")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction

In this project, I replicated the label effect examined in "AI can help people feel heard, but an AI label diminishes this impact" by Yin et al. (2024). In the original paper, the researchers found that 1) AI-generated responses made people feel more heard than human-generated responses; 2) however, people felt less heard when they believed that a response came from AI rather than from a human. In this project, I would focus on replicating the second finding to study the AI label effect.

This study closely fits my research interests because my research mainly focuses on how people interact with AI systems, especially in social and relational contexts. My recent work has focused on the social uses of AI chatbots, and "feeling heard" is closely related to how people use AI systems socially. I am especially interested in the label effect because recently people are increasingly integrating AI systems into their daily lives, at the same time, there is also growing debate about how people perceive the warm and supportive tone of these systems. For example, recent work has raised concerns about behaviors such as sycophancy. This makes me interested in whether simply knowing that a response comes from AI could be an significant factor shaping people's perceptions.

The original study used a 2 (response source: human vs. AI) × 2 (label: human vs. AI) between-subjects design. Participants first described a complex situation they were dealing with. Participants then received responses written either by other humans or by AI (Bing chat with OpenAI GPT-4 model), which were independently labeled as human-generated or AI-generated. Considering the limited budget and the potential risk of participant attrition in a multi-session design, I simplified the replication to a two-condition between-subjects experiment, and I would only focus on the part of the second research question in the original paper, the label effect specifically for AI-generated responses. All participants received AI-generated responses for their shared complex condition. However, the response would be randomly labeled as AI-generated or human-generated. For current setting, the entire experiment was conducted in a single session, allowing participants to describe their sitaution, receiving the response, and the self-reported survey questions align each step follow the original study setup.

I preregistered a two-sided Welch's t-test comparing "feeling heard" scores between the AI-label and human-label conditions as the key statistical test. Consistent with the findings of the original paper, I hypothesized that participants in the AI-label condition would report feeling less heard than those in the human-label condition. 

## Methods

### Power analysis

In the original paper, the authors reported Cohen's $d = 0.52$ for the labeling effect on feeling heard among participants receiving AI-generated responses. I calculated the sample sizes to achieve 80%, 90%, and 95% statistical power to detect the effect size reported in the original paper, as well as the sample size required using the 2.5× original sample size approach (Simonsohn, 2015; Experimentology §10.4). Given the course's budget constraints, I targeted a final sample of 146 participants (73 per condition) for analysis, providing approximately 88% power to detect the original effect size.

```{r}
#| label: power
# Effect to detect: Cohen's d reported by the original paper for the AI-response comparison
# (SI Table 2, Feeling Heard, AI response human label - AI response AI label: d = 0.52, 95% CI [0.31, 0.74]).
original_d <- 0.52

power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  n <- power.t.test(delta = original_d, sd = 1,
                    power = pw, sig.level = 0.05)$n
  tibble(power = scales::percent(pw), n_per_group = ceiling(n), n_total = 2 * ceiling(n))
})

two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original$n)
power_rows <- power_rows |>
  mutate(across(everything(), as.character)) |>
  bind_rows(tibble(power = "2.5 x original sample (Simonsohn, 2015)",
                   n_per_group = paste(two_and_half, collapse = " / "),
                   n_total = as.character(sum(two_and_half))))

knitr::kable(power_rows, col.names = c("Power", "N per label condition", "N total"),
             caption = sprintf(
               "Sample needed to detect the original effect (Feeling Heard among AI-generated responses, AI label vs. human label, Cohen's d = %.2f from SI Table 2), two-sided alpha = .05. The last row is 2.5 times the original cell sizes (AI label / human label).",
               original_d))
```

### Planned sample

We targeted 146 participants for the final analysis and planned to recruit through Prolific. Consistent with the original study, we would restrict participants to US residents who reported English as their first language and were at least 18 years old. Data collection would stop once we received 146 valid submissions that all met the inclusion criteria. The study was conducted in a single session, with a median completion time of approximately 7 minutes in the pilot. The compensation was \$1.40 per participant, equivalent to about \$12 per hour based on the pilot median, which meets Prolific's recommended payment.


### Materials

First, participants were asked to describe a complex situation they were currently experiencing, following the exact same instructions as in the original paper: "Please take a moment to think about a complex situation that you are grappling with. This might involve a challenging decision or issue in either your personal or professional life, characterized by numerous interwoven factors. You might be dealing with an interpersonal conflict involving colleagues, family members, or friends, and are uncertain about the best course of action. You might be wrestling with a profound question or thought."

Since my replication focused on the labeling effect among AI-generated responses, all responses were generated using a large language model (LLM) through an API call with the following prompt, following the original paper: "A person you otherwise don't know described the following complex situation they have been dealing with. Please respond to what they said in a way that makes them feel understood. Keep your response to 57 words. '[description]'" we set the target response length to 57 words, which is the median of the six batch-level median response lengths reported in the original paper.

The remaining survey questions mainly followed the original study in both wording and order, with minor adjustments to reflect the updated AI systems and survey format. After describing their complex situation, participants rated the extent to which they experienced six emotions (happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust) on a 7-point scale before being assigned to a label condition. Participants were then randomly assigned to either the AI-label or human-label condition and received instructions describing the supposed identity of their conversation partner. In the AI-label condition, participants were told: "Next, you will have a live chat with an AI chatbot. What you just wrote will be sent to the chatbot, and we will ask the chatbot to respond to what you said." In the human-label condition, participants were told: "Next, you will have a live chat with another participant on Prolific who is taking part in this study right now. What you just wrote will be sent to the participant, and we will ask the participant to respond to what you said." The wording differed only in how the response source was described: "the AI chatbot's response" in the AI-label condition and "another Prolific participant's response" in the human-label condition. Both versions ended with the same statement: "We are interested in your impressions of the response." After receiving the AI-generated response, participants completed the same outcome measures as in the original study, including feeling heard, perceived response accuracy, perceived responder understanding, and feeling of connection to the responder. Participants then answered questions about their emotional state, including their current emotions, loneliness, and questions about the perception and usage toward AI. We replaced references to "Bing Chat" in the original study with the more general term "AI chatbot." Finally, participants completed questions measuring their suspicion about the source of the response, and demographic questions. At the end, we would provide the debriefing of the study and tell everyone that all the messages were generated by an AI system. 



### Procedure

We adapted the procedure from the original study. However, unlike the original study, which involved three stages and required participants to return to read their responses, our replication was conducted entirely in a single session. Participants first provided informed consent and entered their Prolific ID. They then read the study instructions and were asked to describe a complex situation they were currently experiencing. Unlike the original study, which asked participants to record an audio description, participants typed their descriptions into a text box on the survey page. To get enough information, we required users to describe their situation in at least 30 words. After submitting their descriptions, participants rated the six emotions they experienced in the situation.

After completing the emotion ratings, participants were randomly assigned to either the AI-label or human-label condition using Qualtrics, with approximately equal numbers of participants assigned to each condition. Then, depending on their assigned condition, we told participants that they would have a live chat with either an AI chatbot or another Prolific participant currently taking part in the study. On the following page, participants would chat with an embedded chat interface, which included a message describing the complex situation the participants experienced. Each participant's description was sent to the same LLM using the same prompt, regardless of the assigned label, and one personalized response was generated through an API call when the chat page loaded. The response appeared after a 20–25-second wait in both conditions to make the human-labeled response appear more realistic.

After reading the response, participants completed the outcome measures, including feeling heard, perceived response accuracy, perceived responder understanding, and connection to the responder. They then answered questions about their current loneliness and 19 emotions, followed by trait loneliness, mind perception of AI, and familiarity with, use of, and attitudes toward AI chatbots. Next, participants completed a question measuring their suspicion about the response's source, demographic questions, instruction clarity, and optional comments. Finally, participants received a debrief explaining that all responses were AI-generated regardless of the assigned label.

The entire study was completed in a single session. In the pilot, the median completion time was approximately 7 minutes.


### Analysis plan

First, we will exclude participants who do not complete the survey, do not provide valid consent, or have missing responses to any of the six feeling-heard questions. Following the original study, participants must provide a sufficiently detailed description of their situation. In our replication, we require a minimum of 30 words when participants describe their situation.

Our primary analysis will examine whether labeling an AI-generated response as AI rather than human affects participants' feeling of being heard. Following the original study, we will calculate the mean of the six feeling-heard items for each participant. We will then conduct a two-sided Welch's t-test comparing the AI-label and human-label conditions, using $\alpha = 0.05$. Considering the original study's results, we hypothesize that participants in the AI-label condition will report lower levels of feeling heard than those in the human-label condition. We will report the difference in means, its 95% confidence interval, and Cohen's $d$.

In addition, we will conduct exploratory analyses examining the effect of labeling on the other three outcomes from the original study, including perceived response accuracy, perceived responder understanding, and feeling of connection to the responder. We will compare these outcomes between the two conditions using Welch's t-tests. 


### Differences from the original study

There are five main differences. First, we focused on the labeling effect among AI-generated responses. While the original study used a 2 × 2 design manipulating both the response source (AI vs. human) and the response label (AI vs. human), in this project all responses were generated by AI but randomly labeled as either AI-generated or human-written. Participants were randomly assigned to the two label conditions after completing the initial emotion ratings, with approximately equal numbers assigned to each condition.

Second, we simplified the original three-part procedure into a single-session experiment. Instead of returning the following day to receive a response, participants received an AI-generated response in real time through an embedded chat interface. The interface displayed either a human or AI label and the response to participants' situation. Before showing the response, we intentionally had a 20- to 25-second waiting period in both conditions to make the human-labeled interaction appear more realistic. In the human-labeled condition, participants were told that another Prolific participant was taking part in the study at the same time and would write a response to their situation.

Third, we used GPT-6-luna instead of GPT-4 through Bing Chat, since it was no longer publicly available. Responses were generated through live API calls using the Vegapunk server. We followed the original study's response-generation prompt and asked the model to generate the response to about 57 words, which is consistent with the original paper.

Fourth, different from the original study, we asked participants to type their descriptions of complex situations rather than record an audio message. We required participants to provide at least 30 words and disabled pasting to encourage them to describe their own experience.

Fifth, we made several adjustments to the survey wording and measures. Instead of references to "Bing Chat" in the original survey, we used the more general term "AI chatbot." The primary outcome measures, including feeling heard, response accuracy, responder understanding, and connection, all remain consistent with the original study.

```{r}
#| label: funnel
#| eval: !expr have_data
funnel_levels <- c("Started", "Completed", "Passed exclusion criteria")
bind_rows(
  participants |> mutate(step = "Started"),
  complete     |> mutate(step = "Completed"),
  keep         |> mutate(step = "Passed exclusion criteria")
) |>
  mutate(step = factor(step, levels = funnel_levels)) |>
  mutate(condition = coalesce(condition, "not assigned")) |>
  count(step, condition, .drop = FALSE) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(Total = rowSums(across(-step))) |>
  rename(Step = step) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Participants at each step, by label condition. Differences between labels in attrition or exclusion are a threat to validity and should be discussed.")
```

```{r}
#| label: demographics

# The categories and counts below are from Yin et al. (2024), Methods, "Participants" (p. 8),
# for all 455 recipients (AI and human responses together): gender 221 women, 227 men,
# 6 non-binary, 1 did not report; race/ethnicity 343 White, 55 Black, 26 mixed race, 15 Asian, 11 Hispanic,
# 3 other, 1 Native American, 1 did not report; mean age 43.82 (SD 13.12).
paper_gender <- tibble(category = c("Woman", "Man", "Non-binary", "Other", "Prefer not to say"),
                       paper_n  = c(221, 227, 6, 0, 1))
paper_race   <- tibble(category = c("White", "Black", "Asian", "Hispanic", "Native American",
                                    "Mixed race", "Other", "Prefer not to say"),
                       paper_n  = c(343, 55, 15, 11, 1, 26, 3, 1))

# Qualtrics stores a multiple-choice answer as the number of the choice, in the order the choices were listed
# (qualtrics/build-survey.js, Demographics block).
gender_levels <- c("Woman", "Man", "Non-binary", "Other", "Prefer not to say")
race_levels   <- paper_race$category
for (col in c("age", "gender", "race")) if (!col %in% names(keep)) keep[[col]] <- NA
demo <- keep |>
  transmute(participant_id,
            age    = ifelse(between(as.numeric(age), 18, 120), as.numeric(age), NA_real_),
            gender = gender_levels[as.integer(gender)],
            race   = race_levels[as.integer(race)])

tabulate_category <- function(values, paper) {
  recoded <- ifelse(is.na(values), "Not answered", values)
  tibble(category = recoded) |>
    count(category, name = "this_study") |>
    full_join(paper, by = "category") |>
    mutate(across(c(this_study, paper_n), ~ replace_na(.x, 0)),
           category = factor(category, levels = c(paper$category, "Not answered"))) |>
    arrange(category)
}

# Several tables come out of one chunk, and R only auto-prints the last value of a block, so each
# table is printed explicitly (the chunk uses results: asis).
show_table <- function(k) { cat(k, sep = "\n"); cat("\n\n") }
if (nrow(demo) > 0) {
  demo |>
    summarise(N = n(), `Mean age` = round(mean(age, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
              `SD age` = round(sd(age, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
              `Age not given` = sum(is.na(age)),
              `Original mean age` = 43.82, `Original SD age` = 13.12) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Age of the analysed sample, with the original's values.") |> show_table()
  tabulate_category(demo$gender, paper_gender) |>
    knitr::kable(col.names = c("Gender", "This study", "Original (N = 455)"),
                 caption = "Gender of the analysed sample and the original's counts.") |> show_table()
  tabulate_category(demo$race, paper_race) |>
    knitr::kable(col.names = c("Race / ethnicity", "This study", "Original (N = 455)"),
                 caption = "Race / ethnicity of the analysed sample and the original's counts.") |> show_table()
}
```

## Results


### Data preparation
To run the analysis, we conducted four pilot sessions, with participants randomly assigned to either the human-labeled condition (n = 2) or the AI-labeled condition (n = 2).

```{r}
#| label: data-prep-exclusions
#| eval: !expr have_data
# How many records each exclusion rule of the analysis plan removed. The rules are applied in
# read_phase() (under Key statistics); a participant is counted under the first rule they fail.
st <- phase1$status
rules <- c("Did not finish the survey", "No valid consent", "Description under 30 words",
           "Missing one of the six feeling-heard items")
tibble(
  Step = c("Testing IDs (Qualtrics preview and test responses are dropped by the export)", rules, "Analysed: AI label", "Analysed: human label"),
  n = c(as.character(phase1$n_test),
        map_chr(rules, ~ as.character(sum(st$reason == .x))),
        as.character(sum(st$reason == "Analysed" & st$condition == "ai", na.rm = TRUE)),
        as.character(sum(st$reason == "Analysed" & st$condition == "human", na.rm = TRUE)))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Data preparation: records removed by each exclusion rule, and the analysed N by label.")
```

### Confirmatory analysis


```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
scores <- phase1$scores |> filter(!is.na(feeling_heard))

if (all(c("ai", "human") %in% scores$condition) && all(table(scores$condition) >= 2) &&
    n_distinct(scores$feeling_heard) > 1) {
  # Welch's t test on the Feeling Heard composite; the first group listed is the AI label.
  print(t.test(feeling_heard ~ condition, data = scores))
  label_summary(phase1) |>
    mutate(across(c(mean, sd), ~ round(.x, 2))) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Feeling Heard (1-7) by label condition, analysed participants.")
} else {
  message("Welch t test not run: it needs at least two analysed participants in each label condition, ",
          "and some variation in Feeling Heard; there are ", nrow(scores), " analysed participant(s) so far.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory-effect
#| eval: !expr have_data
# The key test's effect sizes: the difference in means (AI label minus human label) with its 95% CI,
# and Cohen's d with an approximate 95% CI.
rep_stats <- diff_ci(label_summary(phase1))
if (!is.null(rep_stats)) {
  rep_stats |>
    transmute(N, `Difference (AI − human label)` = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              `t(df)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.1f)", statistic, df),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
              `d [95% CI]` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", d, d_low, d_high)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "The key test: label effect on Feeling Heard (Welch t test), with Cohen's d.")
} else {
  message("Effect size table not shown: it needs at least two analysed participants in each label condition.")
}
```

### Replication assessment


::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Judge the replication on effect sizes, not only on whether the key test is significant. Compare
the replication estimate and its interval with the original: does the interval exclude zero, and
does it include the original estimate? A significant result much smaller than the original, or
a non-significant result whose interval still includes the original effect, are both
informative and should be reported as such (Experimentology §3.2).
:::

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
orig <- diff_ci(original)
rep  <- diff_ci(label_summary(phase1))

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original"), rep |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Difference (AI − human label)` = sprintf("%.2f points", estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              `d [95% CI]` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", d, d_low, d_high),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: difference in mean Feeling Heard (1-7), AI label minus human label. d uses the pooled SD of the two label groups; the paper's d = 0.52 uses the SD pooled over all four of its conditions.")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: need at least two analysed participants in each label condition.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(rep)) {
  excludes_zero <- rep$ci_low > 0 | rep$ci_high < 0
  includes_orig <- orig$estimate >= rep$ci_low & orig$estimate <= rep$ci_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's 95%% interval %s zero and %s the original estimate of %.2f points. ",
    if (excludes_zero) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    orig$estimate))
  cat(sprintf("The replication estimate of %.2f points %s the original's 95%% interval [%.2f, %.2f]. ",
              rep$estimate,
              if (rep$estimate >= orig$ci_low & rep$estimate <= orig$ci_high) "lies inside" else "lies outside",
              orig$ci_low, orig$ci_high))
  cat("These facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance: show the original next to your replication

**Every report should have a figure that puts the original finding and your replication side by
side.** It is the single most informative thing in a replication report: a reader can see at a
glance whether the effect came back, and how its size compares. Make it however you can, in
roughly this order of preference:

1. **Replot both from numbers.** Enter the original's summary statistics (means or proportions,
   with SDs, SEs or CIs, and Ns) in the original-study chunk at the top of this file, and plot
   them on the same axes as yours. That is what the demo figure below does.
2. **Replot the original from its data**, if the authors shared it or it is in an open
   repository, using exactly the same plotting code as for your own data.
3. **Show the original figure as an image** next to yours if neither is possible. Save a
   screenshot of it, for example as `writeup/images/original-figure.png`, and lay the two out
   in columns:

   ````markdown
   ::: {layout-ncol=2}
   ![Original: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Figure 1](images/original-figure.png)

   ```{{r}}
   # your replication plot here
   ```
   :::
   ````

Whichever you choose, use the same measure, scale, condition order and error-bar meaning for
both panels, label which is which, and cite the source of the original values or figure in the
caption. If the original reported no variability, say so rather than leaving it out silently.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Feeling Heard (1-7) by label condition, original study and Phase 1 replication. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals. Original: the AI-response conditions of Yin et al. (2024), Table 2, with cell sizes from the authors' OSF data."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
comparison_plot(Original = original, `Phase 1: replication` = label_summary(phase1))
```

### Exploratory analyses


::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Any follow-up analyses (optional). Label them clearly as exploratory: they were not planned, so
they generate hypotheses rather than test them.
:::

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-outcomes
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Exploratory (the analysis plan): the label effect on the other three outcomes of the original,
# each with a Welch t test (AI label minus human label), next to the original's cells.
secondary <- c("response_accuracy", "responder_understood", "connection")
outcome_rows <- function(summ, study) {
  map_dfr(secondary, function(m) {
    s_m <- summ[summ$measure == m, ]
    ai <- s_m[s_m$condition == "ai", ]; hu <- s_m[s_m$condition == "human", ]
    r <- diff_ci(s_m)
    tibble(Outcome = measure_labels[[m]], Study = study,
           `n (AI / human label)` = sprintf("%d / %d", ai$n, hu$n),
           `M (SD), AI label` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", ai$mean, ai$sd),
           `M (SD), human label` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", hu$mean, hu$sd),
           `Difference [95% CI]` = if (is.null(r)) "not computable" else sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", r$estimate, r$ci_low, r$ci_high),
           `t(df)` = if (is.null(r)) "" else sprintf("%.2f (%.1f)", r$statistic, r$df),
           p = if (is.null(r)) "" else format.pval(r$p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
           `d [95% CI]` = if (is.null(r)) "" else sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", r$d, r$d_low, r$d_high))
  })
}
rep_sum <- measure_summaries(phase1)
bind_rows(outcome_rows(original_measures, "Original"), outcome_rows(rep_sum, "Phase 1: replication")) |>
  arrange(factor(Outcome, levels = measure_labels[secondary]), Study) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: label effect on the other three outcomes (1-7), Welch t tests; original = AI-response conditions (Table 2).")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-effects
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Exploratory: label effect (AI label minus human label) on the four outcomes, original (AI-response conditions, Table 2) and Phase 1 replication, with 95% confidence intervals. Outcomes with fewer than two analysed participants per label are not shown."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
effects_plot(Original = measure_effects(original_measures),
             `Phase 1: replication` = measure_effects(rep_sum))
```

```{r}
#| label: manipulation-check
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Exploratory: suspicion about the true source of the reply, 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much), by label. In the AI-label
# group the item asks about suspecting a human wrote it; in the human-label group, about suspecting an AI.
if (!"suspicion" %in% names(keep)) keep$suspicion <- NA
keep |>
  mutate(suspicion = as.numeric(suspicion)) |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  summarise(n = sum(!is.na(suspicion)), Mean = round(mean(suspicion, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
            SD = round(sd(suspicion, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
            `% rating 5 to 7` = round(100 * mean(suspicion >= 5, na.rm = TRUE), 0), .groups = "drop") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: suspicion about the source of the reply, by label (analysed participants).")
```

```{r}
#| label: data-quality
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Qualtrics records no browser errors, so check the things that can go wrong in this design instead: technical
# problems the participant reported, pasting into the description box, and how long the reply took to appear.
for (col in c("tech_issues", "desc_paste_attempts", "wait_ms")) if (!col %in% names(participants)) participants[[col]] <- NA
participants |>
  filter(completed) |>
  summarise(`Finished` = n(),
            `Reported a technical issue (chat)` = sum(as.numeric(tech_issues) == 2, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Tried to paste into the description` = sum(as.numeric(desc_paste_attempts) > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median wait before the reply (s)` = round(median(as.numeric(wait_ms), na.rm = TRUE) / 1000, 1)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Data-quality checks (completers).")
```

that judgment on the replication assessment above: the size of the effect relative to the

Open-ended commentary, none of it long: (a) what the exploratory analyses suggest; (b) what the

# Phase 2: Extension

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance: choosing your extension

Follow the Extension guidelines page on Canvas. In brief:

- **By default the extension is a best-practices modification of your Phase 1 experiment.** If
  your replication did not succeed, it is a **rescue**: address the plausible reasons for the
  failure. If it did succeed, it is an **upgrade**: make the estimate more precise. Typical
  changes are better or more reliable measurement, more trials, a within-participant design
  where that is legitimate, comprehension and manipulation checks, clearer instructions, or a
  larger or better-targeted sample.
- **If your scientific extension pitch was approved at Milestone 3 and your replication
  succeeded, propose that instead:** the original conditions rerun unchanged, plus the one
  added condition or manipulation, with a power analysis for the new comparison.
- On either track you may add exploratory measures **at the end** of the study.
- Every change is listed and tagged by category below; everything else stays identical.

State your track on the line below, and delete the others.
:::

**Track:** Best-practices upgrade / Best-practices rescue / Scientific extension (approved at Milestone 3)

## Rationale

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

One or two paragraphs. For a rescue: what are the plausible reasons Phase 1 did not reproduce the
original result, and how does each change address one of them? For an upgrade: where is the
Phase 1 estimate least precise or least trustworthy, and how will the changes improve it? For a
scientific extension: what question does the added condition answer, and why does it follow from
the original finding?
:::

## Changes from Phase 1

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Every change from the Phase 1 experiment, one per row, each tagged with a category: Measurement,
Trials, Design, Checks, Instructions, Sample, Added condition (scientific track only), or
Exploratory measure (end of study only). If it is not in this table, it does not change: same
materials, wording, procedure, exclusion rule and analysis. The rows below are examples for the
demo; replace them with yours.
:::

| # | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sample | 27 analysed participants | 300 analysed participants (150 per frame) | Phase 1's interval was too wide to distinguish the original effect from a much smaller one. |
| 2 | Checks | No comprehension check | After the choice, participants say how many people are at risk (600) | Confirms participants read the scenario; failures are reported, and excluded only if preregistered. |
| 3 | Exploratory measure | None | At the end: "How confident are you in your choice?" (1–7) | Exploratory only; collected after every confirmatory measure. |

Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.

## Power and sample

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Justify the Phase 2 sample, and **state how you expect the estimate and its precision to compare
with Phase 1**. For an upgrade, plan the sample around the confidence interval you want; for a
rescue, around the power to detect the original effect, or the smallest effect you would still
consider a successful replication; for a scientific extension, around the power to detect the new
comparison. Set `phase2_n_per_group` in the code below; the table uses Phase 1's estimate if you
have it and the original's otherwise.
:::

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
phase2_n_per_group <- 150   # planned analysed participants per label condition in Phase 2

orig_stats <- diff_ci(original)
p1_summary <- if (have_data) label_summary(phase1)
p1_stats   <- if (have_data) diff_ci(p1_summary)
basis <- if (!is.null(p1_stats)) {
  list(summary = p1_summary, source = "Phase 1")
} else {
  list(summary = original, source = "the original study")
}
pooled_sd <- function(s) sqrt(sum((s$n - 1) * s$sd^2) / (sum(s$n) - 2))

# Expected 95% CI half-width on the difference at n per condition.
half_width <- function(n) qt(.975, 2 * n - 2) * pooled_sd(basis$summary) * sqrt(2 / n)
power_at <- function(n, delta, sd) {
  tryCatch(power.t.test(n = n, delta = delta, sd = sd, sig.level = 0.05)$power, error = function(e) NA)
}

rows <- tibble(
  Study = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) "Phase 1 (actual)", "Phase 2 (planned)"),
  `N analysed` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) p1_stats$N, 2 * phase2_n_per_group),
  `95% CI half-width` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("±%.2f points", (p1_stats$ci_high - p1_stats$ci_low) / 2),
                          sprintf("±%.2f points (expected)", half_width(phase2_n_per_group)))
)
knitr::kable(rows, caption = sprintf("Precision of the key estimate, Phase 2 expected values based on %s.", basis$source))

tibble(
  `Effect to detect` = c(sprintf("Original: %.2f points", abs(orig_stats$estimate)),
                         if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("Phase 1: %.2f points", abs(p1_stats$estimate)),
                         sprintf("Half the original: %.2f points", abs(orig_stats$estimate) / 2)),
  `Power at planned N` = scales::percent(c(
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, abs(orig_stats$estimate), pooled_sd(original)),
    if (!is.null(p1_stats)) power_at(phase2_n_per_group, abs(p1_stats$estimate), pooled_sd(p1_summary)),
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, abs(orig_stats$estimate) / 2, pooled_sd(original))
  ), accuracy = 1)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Power of the Phase 2 key test at %d per condition, two-sided alpha = .05.", phase2_n_per_group))
```

## Analysis plan

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

The confirmatory analysis for Phase 2, written before Phase 2 data collection. On the
best-practices tracks this is normally the same key test as Phase 1, run on the Phase 2 data
alone; say whether you will also report a pooled estimate across phases, and label it
exploratory if so. On the scientific track, specify the test for the new comparison. Name the
exclusion rule (unchanged unless it is in the Changes table) and list any exploratory measures.

Run Phase 2 under a new `EXPERIMENT.id` in `experiment.js` (for example `smith2016-phase2`) and
set `experiment_id_phase2` at the top of this file to match, so the two phases' data never mix.
:::

## Results

```{r}
#| label: phase2-notice
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!have_phase2) {
  cat(
    "::: {.callout-warning icon=false}\n",
    "## No Phase 2 data yet\n\n",
    "There are no exported data for `", experiment_id_phase2, "` yet, so the Phase 2 results are ",
    "skipped. Export with `node qualtrics/export-data.js --id ", experiment_id_phase2,
    "` once Phase 2 has run.\n",
    ":::\n", sep = "")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: phase2-results
#| eval: !expr have_phase2
p2_summary <- label_summary(phase2)
p2_stats   <- diff_ci(p2_summary)
cat(sprintf("Phase 2: %d started, %d completed, %d analysed.\n",
            nrow(phase2$participants), nrow(phase2$complete), nrow(phase2$keep)))
if (!is.null(p2_stats)) {
  p_text <- if (p2_stats$p < 0.001) "p < .001" else sprintf("p = %.3f", p2_stats$p)
  cat(sprintf("Key comparison: %.2f points [%.2f, %.2f], t(%.1f) = %.2f, %s.\n",
              p2_stats$estimate, p2_stats$ci_low, p2_stats$ci_high,
              p2_stats$df, p2_stats$statistic, p_text))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-phase2
#| eval: !expr have_phase2
#| fig-cap: "Feeling Heard (1-7) by label condition: original study, Phase 1 replication, and Phase 2 extension. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
comparison_plot(Original = original,
                `Phase 1: replication` = if (have_data) label_summary(phase1),
                `Phase 2: extension` = label_summary(phase2))
```
